en: [ACT III]
Same set. Three weeks later.
[SCENE I]
GERTRUDE, EUSTACHE, ADRIEN : (Gertrude is reading in a corner of the room; she should give the impression of being at home; Adrien, who has just arrived, has not taken off his overcoat.)
ADRIEN : Your wife isn't here?

EUSTACHE : Béatrice went to spend two days in Dreux with a friend. She won't be back until dinner. In her absence Gertrude came to keep me company. (A short silence. Adrien is clearly waiting for Gertrude to make up her mind to leave the room; it is obvious she has no intention of doing so.) Is Léontine well?
ADRIEN : Perfectly... that is to say, she's a bit nervous at the moment. Quite understandable... in her condition...
EUSTACHE : I had no idea... congratulations. Mother hadn't told us anything...

ADRIEN : She's only known for a few days. We weren't in any great hurry to tell her... At her age people fuss, they give advice right and left... You have to put yourself in Titine's shoes, it's exhausting. And that's actually partly what brings me here... (He glances in Gertrude's direction.) By the way, how many bedrooms do you have here?
EUSTACHE, surprised : Three bedrooms... no, four, counting the maid's room.
ADRIEN : Do you have guests staying with you right now? Those Boches...
EUSTACHE : Please, Adrien... Werner has left; he's in a boarding house.
ADRIEN : I thought there were two of them.
EUSTACHE : His wife left him.
ADRIEN : Ah, well, that moves fast, just like in the movies...
EUSTACHE : I don't quite understand. (Another glance from Adrien in Gertrude's direction.) You can speak quite freely in front of Gertrude, you know; she's practically family.

ADRIEN, surprised : Really?... Oh, well, I won't beat around the bush. Titine's pregnancy looks like it's going to be a bit difficult; the doctor says she must be spared in every respect. I tell you again, Mother gets on her nerves; it's not the poor old thing's fault, but it seems to me after all that since you have the room... If you took Mother in here for a while... Eh? What do you say? It would just be a temporary arrangement. Later on, we'll see. (A silence.)
EUSTACHE : Does Mother know about this approach of yours?

ADRIEN : Of course not. Besides, there's no question of any formal approach. I understand perfectly that you have to talk to your wife about it first. It's obvious she has a say in the matter. But deep down she puts up with Mother better than Titine does. When Mother comes home from your place, she's always delighted; she makes a tremendous fuss over Béatrice's virtues, and that's also something that annoys my little kitten a bit; quite understandable, in a way... Personally, I need peace and quiet in my own home. I hate bickering. Business gives me enough headaches as it is. When I come home, I need peace. Those kinds of worries, you don't know what they're like, and you're very lucky... Yes, I know, you have your rallies, your articles; but that keeps you busy, it stirs up your bile a bit, it serves as fencing practice for you. By the way, I saw your name again at the bottom of that rag... what were you protesting against again?... the crackdown on communist activities in Yugoslavia. Good grief, you really must have time to waste to get worked up over Yugoslav communists!... Still, if you didn't have some so-called injustice somewhere to protest against every week, you'd die of boredom, and maybe of constipation... it keeps you in good health, that's the main thing, after all... As for me, I'm not worried... communism in France isn't happening anytime soon.
EUSTACHE, who has exchanged glances and sighs with Gertrude : I will think over what you've asked... unfortunately I'm not sure circumstances lend themselves to what you want.
ADRIEN : Is there news in your household, too?
EUSTACHE : Not in the sense you mean.

ADRIEN : Well then... If I were in your shoes, I know I'd find it only natural to shoulder my share of the burden (Gertrude bursts out laughing, then quickly stifles it). But then, everyone is their own judge in these matters. And besides, I suppose you see friends of your in-laws, posh people, very fashionable... Obviously the poor old thing isn't exactly presentable.
EUSTACHE : Adrien! Do you really imagine?...
ADRIEN : You have to see things as they are. Why, when we have company for dinner, she herself asks to eat in her room. As long as we save her a bit of vol-au-vent or a few petits fours...
EUSTACHE : That is horrible...

ADRIEN : What's horrible about it?... Anyway, the two of you can look into it and call me. It's mainly because of Titine... Otherwise, I'll have to make other arrangements. There's no shortage of decent retirement homes, only they're still quite expensive, and I'm afraid she'd be bored.
EUSTACHE : That's out of the question.

ADRIEN : It's so much in question that that's how it will end up if you don't make up your mind... Well, goodbye. (He goes toward the door.) (In an undertone.) Tell me, that woman—what the devil is she doing here? Eh?...
EUSTACHE, pretending not to have heard : Goodbye, give Mother my love.
ADRIEN : Rather than kissing her... (The rest is lost.)
[SCENE II]
GERTRUDE : Well?
EUSTACHE : We'll see.

GERTRUDE : He's quite something, your brother... But if he imagines his tailor can keep him from looking like a department manager at the Galeries Lafayette... He looks like you, though... better looking than you, but he looks like you. Kiss me. You're sulking!...
EUSTACHE : I'm rather troubled... I don't want them dumping her in Sainte-Perrine at all...
GERTRUDE : Your wife will take her in perhaps; she has all the makings of a Newfoundland rescue dog.
EUSTACHE : Don't talk nonsense, please.
GERTRUDE : Deep down I rather like it when you sulk. After all, it's your natural expression. When you smile, I don't recognize you. You strike me as posing.
EUSTACHE : Me, a poseur!

GERTRUDE : No, you fool! Posing like at the photographer's. But maybe little by little you'll get a natural look. Then I'll get used to it. We won't be bored, the two of us... Eh? Not saying anything?
EUSTACHE : I feel no need to add to that...
GERTRUDE : Such dread of useless words! It isn't like sending mail, though; there's no surcharge to pay.
EUSTACHE : When I think about what has happened over the past three weeks...
GERTRUDE : Well?
EUSTACHE : You will still have to tell me once and for all...
GERTRUDE : Again!
EUSTACHE : Yes. If it was blackmail, perhaps I can accept it, but only on condition that you admit it.
GERTRUDE : Always like at the post office. Having to sign ledgers, asking for receipts. It's infuriating.
EUSTACHE : Until now I thought we agreed on holding to a certain honesty.
GERTRUDE : There are things so much more important... Aren't there?
EUSTACHE : That depends on the point of view one takes.
GERTRUDE : You sound so utterly naive right now... Your whole education has yet to begin.
EUSTACHE : Thank you.
GERTRUDE : It has begun. In a fortnight, you've already made great progress. (She laughs.)
EUSTACHE : Why are you laughing? -
GERTRUDE : I'm thinking of your wife. She would be quite surprised...
EUSTACHE : Probably much less than you think.
GERTRUDE : Really?
EUSTACHE : She has certainly guessed.
GERTRUDE : Well now!
EUSTACHE : Yes, when I came back from your place, that first day...
GERTRUDE : Did she say something?
EUSTACHE : Simply: "I won't ask you for news of the rue Froidevaux. I can see clearly that your mind is completely at ease."
GERTRUDE : And so you think?...
EUSTACHE : That's my impression. And since then, two or three times... I can't even call them digs.
GERTRUDE : That's curious.
EUSTACHE : You seem disappointed.
GERTRUDE : Not at all, only I wonder...
EUSTACHE : If she went to spend two days in Dreux, I think it was to think things over...
GERTRUDE : Who is this friend of hers?
EUSTACHE : A sort of former governess she is very fond of.
GERTRUDE : Heavens! I can see her from here.
EUSTACHE : What a vivid imagination!... Through all of this, you haven't answered me.
GERTRUDE : It's very hard to know. The idea had crossed my mind...
EUSTACHE : What idea?
GERTRUDE : Well, I'd bought a tube of Veronal... I didn't quite know yet what I'd do with it... All in all, I didn't lie to you. And besides, I'm too happy.
EUSTACHE : That first day, with the decorator... (He has approached Gertrude) you must have been very happy then, too.
GERTRUDE : Leave me alone about Roger.
EUSTACHE : I ran into him on the stairs. A well-built fellow. (He pinches her.)
GERTRUDE : What a brute!
[SCENE III]
THE SAME, DURAND-FRESNEL.
DURAND-FRESNEL, entering with his hat on : Where is Béatrice?
EUSTACHE : You know perfectly well she's in Dreux until this evening.
DURAND-FRESNEL : People walk into your house like a public thoroughfare, it's unbelievable.
EUSTACHE : You know Madame Heuzard... My father-in-law.
DURAND-FRESNEL, after giving the most discourteous nod of the head to Gertrude : I have a rather particular matter to discuss with you... What I learned earlier is unbelievable.
GERTRUDE : It must be unbelievably late. Goodbye, Eustache.
EUSTACHE : Stay a little longer.
DURAND-FRESNEL : Is it true that, not content with turning down a promotion that, at the request of a friend of mine...
EUSTACHE : Ah?
DURAND-FRESNEL : Most certainly: of a friend of mine... the minister had been good enough to grant you, you wrote him a most insulting letter?
EUSTACHE : I have heard you call him a boor.
GERTRUDE, bursting out laughing : Goodbye. Until tomorrow. Five o'clock at the Régence, remember.
EUSTACHE : Agreed. I won't see you out. (Gertrude exits.)
[SCENE IV]
DURAND-FRESNEL : That person has a strange manner. I ask you to explain yourself.
EUSTACHE : About her presence here?
DURAND-FRESNEL : Certainly not. That lady does not interest me in the slightest.
EUSTACHE : Very well.

DURAND-FRESNEL : Conduct such as yours is worthy of the Bolsheviks... Perhaps those people are your friends; they will never be mine. Yesterday in Le Temps I read reports that gave me goose pimples. An old liberal like myself... But what I cannot accept is that at the precise moment when ties of friendship are being reformed between Republican Unionists and Unionist Republicans, you take it upon yourself to deliver a downright slap in the face to a man I esteem, an old comrade.
EUSTACHE : I think it preferable to warn you that this is only a beginning; yes, I have undertaken a kind of general housecleaning, and before long you will be hearing more.
DURAND-FRESNEL : Housecleaning! Housecleaning! Now there is a word whose ring strikes me as terribly un-republican; remember the execrable use our worst adversaries have made of it, Eustache...
EUSTACHE : There is no reason to leave them a monopoly on it. I have had enough, do you hear me, of being patronized by your little cronies. From this day forward, all bridges are burned.
DURAND-FRESNEL : May one know what you mean by that?
[SCENE V]
THE SAME, BÉATRICE.
BÉATRICE : Hello, Eustache. Why, are you here, Papa?

DURAND-FRESNEL : Béatrice, I advise you to keep a weather eye open. Your husband is preparing to do something foolish. Though I don't know exactly what. I advise you to recall him to a more accurate awareness of what he owes to all of us. Oh, I make no allusion to the services I may personally have rendered him; that is not my way. But it seems to me...
BÉATRICE : I think you are wasting your breath, Papa. Even assuming I agreed with you, I am not at all sure I could still obtain from Eustache...
DURAND-FRESNEL : You surprise me right now. Do you not represent, in your husband's eyes...
BÉATRICE : Please... That is precisely what must no longer be said or thought...

DURAND-FRESNEL : You are making me lose my train of thought. You are unbearable. I shall tell your mother to telephone you this evening. She will certainly know how to make herself heard. It's unbelievable...
BÉATRICE : Papa, right now you are like a caricature of yourself. Dear God, how dreadful! Is there really nothing in life but puppets and... and the desperate?
DURAND-FRESNEL : I am not a desperate man, my child. I believe in reason and progress. Goodbye. (He exits.)
[SCENE VI]
BÉATRICE : Did everything go well in my absence?
EUSTACHE : As well as could be. Did you have a good journey?
BÉATRICE : Those Citroën buses are convenient, though one suffocates a bit in them.
EUSTACHE : Was your friend pleased to see you?
BÉATRICE : I think so... But I found her aged, shrunken; it grieved me. (A silence.) Who left her little handbag here?
EUSTACHE : That must be Gertrude.
BÉATRICE : Rather an elegant little handbag.
EUSTACHE : I gave it to her last week.
BÉATRICE : Oh?... She was here earlier?
EUSTACHE, looking her straight in the face : She spent thirty-six hours here with me.
BÉATRICE : That is perfectly clear.
EUSTACHE : It seems to me.
BÉATRICE : I am not very surprised.
EUSTACHE : No.
BÉATRICE : And now? (A gesture from Eustache.) What does that gesture mean?
EUSTACHE : Certain decisions will have to be made.
BÉATRICE : As far as you are concerned, I must assume that has already been done.
EUSTACHE : Yes... All the same, we must come to an understanding. (A quiet laugh from Béatrice.) An entire period of our life is coming to an end.
BÉATRICE : You don't sound very cheerful saying that.
EUSTACHE : I am not cheerful.
BÉATRICE : I, at least, am... perfectly calm.
EUSTACHE : Implausibly calm.
BÉATRICE : Were you expecting a scene, Eustache?
EUSTACHE : I don't know... I am glad you are not suffering.
